UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al.
Large Loads Co-Located at Generating Facilities
Constellation Energy Generation, LLC
     v.
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.
)
)
)
)

)
)
Docket No. EL25-49-000
Docket No. EL25-49-001
Docket No. AD24-11-000
Docket No. EL25-20-000
(Consolidated)
MOTION FOR LEAVE AND ANSWER OF  
CONSTELLATION ENERGY GENERATION, LLC 
Constellation moves for leave and submits this answer1 to reject four arguments made by 
PJM and the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners in their response briefs.2 First, just and 
reasonable rules for large load interconnection cannot be delayed until the end of the decade and 
claims that such delays are “required”3 are belied both by PJM’s rush to adopt its own preferred 
“Connect and Manage” alternative and by the fact that other regions are managing to develop rules 
for interruptibility much more quickly. Second, the Federal Power Act (“FPA”) requires study 
requirements to be clearly written in the PJM Tariff because these study timelines and 
methodologies significantly affect the provision of the new transmission services—and a lack of 
1 Constellation Energy Generation, LLC (“Constellation”) submits this answer and motion for leave pursuant to 
Rules 212 and 213 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212 and 385.213. 
Constellation respectfully submits there is good cause for the Commission to accept this answer as it is intended to 
aid the Commission in its decision-making. Unless otherwise defined, all capitalized terms have the same meaning 
as in PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 (2025) (“December 18th Order”). 
2 Reply Brief of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. at 57 (Apr. 24, 2026) (“PJM Apr. 24 Response”); Reply Brief of the 
Indicated PJM Transmission Owners (Apr. 24, 2026) (“Indicated TO Apr. 24 Response”). The Indicated PJM 
Transmission Owners (“Transmission Owners”) that filed the Indicated TO Apr. 24 Response are the same subset 
of Transmission Owners in PJM that filed the February 23, 2026 Initial Brief and March 25, 2026 Reply. 
3 PJM Apr. 24 Response at 57.

2 
clarity and resulting protracted delays (including delays due to refusals to study) are what 
instigated this proceeding in the first place. Third, draconian rules imposing disqualifications, 
suspensions and other unnecessary restrictions on the Commission’s new transmission services do 
not address any genuine “risks to reliability and resource adequacy”4 but instead merely limit 
access to, frustrate, and otherwise discriminate against these landmark services. Fourth, the 
Transmission Owners’ excessive Grid Reliance Charge has no basis in principle or precedent, 
while Constellation has proposed a just and reasonable replacement rate the Commission can 
readily adopt. In addition, there are several other areas in PJM’s response brief and revised 
Illustrative Tariff where clarification is needed or appropriate. 
I.
Three Years Is Not “Required” to Replace an Unlawful Rate 
PJM claims “[a] June 1, 2029 effective date is required for the provision of these new, 
curtailable services.”5 At the same time, PJM is expediting its Connect and Manage 
interconnection framework to commence June 1, 2027, which would allow the interconnection of 
non-capacity backed loads that are potentially interruptible during capacity shortages, unless the 
load brings its own (new) generation.6 This, ironically, is a rebranded Option 7 from PJM’s show-
cause filing, which the Commission rejected in favor of Interim Network Integration Transmission 
Service (“Interim NITS”).7 PJM did not seek rehearing on this point, yet PJM is nonetheless fast-
tracking the version of interruptibility that the Commission rejected, while slow-boating the 
4 Id. at 45. 
5 Id. at 57. 
6 PJM, Connect & Manage Exemption and Reliability Backstop Process Impacts, Connect and Manage Senior Task 
Force, at 2 (Apr. 28, 2026), 20260428-item-03---connect--manage-exemption-and-reliability-backstop-process-
impacts-education---presentation.pdf (“Connect & Manage Presentation”). 
7 December 18th Order, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 200 (“we direct PJM to submit, within 60 days of the date of issuance 
of this order, a compliance filing to create a new interim, non-firm transmission service similar, but not identical, to 
PJM’s proposed option 7.”).

3 
version of interruptibility that the Commission required. That is unacceptable. It is simply not 
credible that PJM will take more than three years to implement Interim NITS allegedly due to 
“significant changes to PJM’s core Markets and Operations systems”8 but less than one year to 
commence Connect and Manage, a framework not clearly defined let alone demonstrated to be 
just and reasonable.  
Accordingly, the Commission should promptly approve the rates and terms for Interim 
NITS, with Constellation’s focused modifications,9 and make them effective no later than 
October 1, 2026, so that service can begin no later than June 1, 2027, the same date that PJM plans 
to commence Connect and Manage. Adopting Interim NITS as soon as possible—for pending and 
future NITS applicants—should not be difficult. PJM “designed the new Interim NITS to basically 
be treated the same as regular, full NITS.”10
II.
Study Procedures and Deadlines Must Be in the Tariff 
The study procedures for the new transmission services must be identified clearly and 
spelled out in the tariff. Indeed, additional studies may not be needed at all to implement Interim 
NITS. As PJM states, it could determine that “the NITS study already conclusively answers the 
question of whether and how much Interim NITS may be provided” and grant Interim NITS 
“immediately.”11 PJM nevertheless argues, first, that its Illustrative Tariff properly details how 
8 PJM Apr. 24 Response at 57. 
9 Response Brief of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC at 7 (Apr. 24, 2026) (“Constellation Apr. 24 Response”); 
see also Reply Brief of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC at 14-25, 29 (Mar. 25, 2026) (“Constellation Mar. 25 
Reply”). 
10 PJM Apr. 24 Response at 1. 
11 Id. at 27.

4 
PJM will study requests for new transmission services.12 Second, PJM claims that load integration 
studies are outside the scope of the Commission’s jurisdiction.13 Neither argument has merit. 
A. The Commission Should Require Clear and Detailed Study Requirements to 
be on File 
The Illustrative Tariff does not contain any clear statement of what studies will be required 
for the new transmission services. Rather, it states merely that PJM will determine “whether 
additional studies are needed”14 for Interim NITS and “will coordinate with the affected 
Transmission Owner(s) to complete studies, including load integration studies”15 for Contract 
Demand Services. Contrary to PJM’s assertions, these vague statements do not come close to 
“appropriately detail[ing] PJM’s process, role, and standards for studying requests for these new 
transmission services.”16 Indeed, the only “detail” that can be gleaned from the Illustrative Tariff 
is that studies may be conducted. There is no indication of what type of studies will be conducted—
other than the Transmission Owners’ load integration studies—or the methodologies PJM will use 
to assess whether the transmission system can “reliably” provide the new transmission services.  
These are not mere “implementation” details that are missing from the Illustrative Tariff. 
These terms directly affect eligibility for Interim NITS and Contract Demand Services, which 
clearly is a core requirement of the service.17 Requirements establishing the type of studies 
performed and methodologies used to assess whether PJM can provide the new transmission 
12 Id. at 22. 
13 Id. at 34. 
14 Illustrative Tariff, Part XI, § 704.1. 
15 Id. at § 710.3. 
16 PJM Apr. 24 Response at 22. 
17 December 18th Order, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 200 (“Moreover, this new service would be optional for an Eligible 
Customer seeking NITS on behalf of a Co-Located Load and would only be available to the extent PJM determines 
that it can provide some level of interim service reliably.”) (emphasis added).

5 
services reliably are “practices that affect rates and service significantly, that are realistically 
susceptible of specification, and that are not so generally understood in any contractual 
arrangement as to render recitation superfluous.”18 PJM has a “statutory obligation to file 
significant changes to its rates and ‘practices … affecting such rates.’”19 It is irrelevant whether 
stakeholders have the “fulsome opportunity to participate”20 in the development of PJM’s Manuals 
because including this material is part of PJM’s compliance obligation.21 
Accordingly, the Commission should direct PJM to set forth clear and specific study 
requirements in the Tariff. At a minimum, PJM should specify in its Tariff the violations that will 
be studied and the studies to be conducted for each, the deadline for completing each study and 
steps taken if study deadlines are not met, and defined remediation for specific violations found. 
The record in this long proceeding underscores that it is critical for these study rules and deadlines 
to be on file to effectuate the Commission’s and the Trump Administration’s commitment to 
providing prompt service to large loads.22
18 City of Cleveland v. FERC, 773 F.2d 1368, 1376 (D.C. Cir. 1985) (emphasis in original). 
19 Keyspan-Ravenswood, LLC v. FERC, 474 F.3d 804, 811 (D.C. Cir. 2007) (internal quotations omitted). 
20 PJM Apr. 24 Response at 33. 
21 See December 18th Order, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 219 (requesting briefing on rates, terms, and conditions for the 
new transmission services); see also Keyspan-Ravenswood, LLC v. FERC, 474 F.3d at 811 (“[T]he Commission 
provides no reason to believe that Ravenswood’s participation in such a stakeholder process relieved NYISO of its 
statutory obligation to file significant changes to its rates and ‘practices … affecting such rates.’”). 
22 See, e.g., Constellation Complaint at 7 (“Exelon is refusing to process necessary studies on these grounds, 
demanding expensive upgrades under their unfiled interconnection procedures, delaying agreed-upon work which 
will force a nuclear plant to take additional outages, and forcing additional services to be procured.”); id. at 7-8. 
(“Exelon fulfilled its responsibilities as an interconnection provider to review PJM’s necessary studies for one 
Constellation nuclear station, the LaSalle Clean Energy Center (‘LaSalle’), but later refused to do so at the other two 
stations, insisting that Constellation or its potential customer must first apply for retail service and designate what 
sort of wholesale transmission service it will take from Exelon.”); id. at 17 (“But for Constellation’s … Limerick 
Clean Energy Center (‘Limerick’) in Pennsylvania, Exelon has refused to conduct its review of PJM’s completed 
necessary studies, insisting that Constellation or its potential customer must first apply for retail service and 
designate what sort of wholesale transmission service it will take from Exelon.”); id. at 8 (“projects are being held 
hostage by a few monopolies refusing to cooperate with reliability studies related to interconnection modifications”); 
id. at 10 n.25 (“Exelon refuses to review co-location reliability studies as required by the OATT and pro forma ISA”)

6 
B. Transmission Owner Load Integration Study Requirements are Unwritten 
and Undisclosed Policies that Significantly Affect the Commission’s 
Landmark Transmission Services 
The Commission has jurisdiction to regulate load integration studies in connection with 
jurisdictional transmission service. PJM is wrong to assert that “any ‘lack of detail’” regarding 
those studies is justified for jurisdictional reasons.23 The Commission has jurisdiction over all 
transmissions, including transmissions to end users.24 The courts have long held the Commission 
can regulate practices affecting rates within its jurisdiction, even if the Commission’s regulation 
touches upon state authority.25 Load integration studies, which determine “whether (and to what 
(citing Constellation PDO Protest, Exhibit 1, Declaration of James R. McCoskey at ¶ 13); id. at 16 (“Proposed Fully 
Isolated Co-Located data center projects in PJM are currently being held hostage by one or two monopoly utilities’ 
refusal to cooperate … with reliability studies related to interconnection modifications.”); see also Constellation 
Energy Generation, LLC November 21, 2025 Supporting Comments, Docket No. RM26-4-000 at 3-4 (Nov. 21, 
2025) (“Some Transmission Owners have simply refused to participate in PJM’s studies to analyze reliability 
impacts; and some, acting under unfiled interconnection study procedures, have changed their entire construct and 
timetable for processing load studies.”); Answer of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC, PJM Interconnection, 
L.L.C. et al., Docket Nos. EL25-49-000, et al., at 3 (Apr. 23, 2025) (“The Indicated Transmission Owners read the 
existing Tariff to require this one-size-fits-all limitation, and they have refused to perform studies for new load 
seeking a different configuration.”) (“Constellation Apr. 23, 2025 Answer”); id. at 14 (“What is more, regardless of 
what the Tariff actually says and does not say, some of the Indicated Transmission Owners have refused to cooperate 
in PJM’s ‘necessary studies’ process unless the load agrees to taking NITS, claiming justification under the Tariff. 
Some of the Indicated Transmission Owners have refused to process necessary studies, demanded expensive 
upgrades under their unfiled interconnection procedures, and forced a generator seeking to serve co-located load to 
procure additional services not required by the Tariff.”) (citing Constellation Complaint at 7); Constellation 
Complaint at 9 (“Exelon’s also is refusing to perform work on LaSalle’s interconnection facilities to accommodate 
co-location, none of which affects the grid. Exelon’s refusal to complete previously agreed-upon work as scheduled 
during an upcoming planned outage will increase costs to Constellation by $15.3-$19 million at that site alone, just 
so Exelon can pursue its litigation positions.”); see also PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 190 FERC ¶ 61,115, at P 75 
(2025) (“[T]here are allegations in the record that Exelon has delayed work on Constellation’s requests to co-locate 
load with its generators at certain facilities due to Exelon’s concerns that such requests are not allowed under the 
Tariff without arranging for wholesale transmission or retail distribution service.”). 
23 PJM Apr. 24 Response at 34 (“at root, … Constellation’s complaints regarding the level of detail in PJM’s study 
procedures generally concern the Transmission Owner’s load integration studies”). 
24 16 U.S.C. § 824(a); New York v. FERC, 535 U.S. 1, 20 (2002) (“[T]he FPA authorizes FERC’s jurisdiction over 
interstate transmissions, without regard to whether the transmissions are sold to a reseller or directly to a 
consumer.”); December 18th Order, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at PP 170, 173-74. 
25 See, e.g., New Eng. Power Generators Ass’n v. FERC, 757 F.3d 283, 290-91 (D.C. Cir. 2014) (upholding the 
Commission’s mitigation of buyer-side market power as to out-of-market entrants as not “improperly regulating 
‘facilities used for the generation of electric energy”); id. at 290 (“We have previously held that the Commission has 
jurisdiction to regulate certain parameters of the capacity market related to the price of capacity, even if those 
determinations touch on states’ authority.”); Conn. Dep’t of Pub. Util Control v. FERC, 569 F.3d 477, 481-83

7 
level)” the new transmission services can be reliably provided (that is, whether the new 
transmission services are provided at all), easily fall within that scope.26
On rehearing, and on its own accord,27 the Commission should exercise its jurisdiction over 
the load integration studies needed to provide jurisdictional transmission service and direct those 
load integration studies to be on file.28 At a minimum, the PJM Tariff should specify the violations 
that will be studied and the studies to be conducted for each, the deadline for completing each 
study and steps taken if study deadlines are not met, and define remediation for specific violations 
found. Otherwise, the Commission risks neutering its December 18th Order by allowing 
recalcitrant Transmission Owners an avenue to delay or disfavor the Commission’s new 
transmission services.29
III.
The Commission Should Reject Certain Proposed Strictures on the New Transmission 
Services 
PJM claims that its draconian disqualification and suspension scheme is necessary to 
address “unique reliability and resource adequacy risks” of integrating large loads into PJM’s 
(upholding Commission’s authority to regulate the Installed Capacity Requirement, even if the requirement could 
necessitate the construction of facilities, a matter traditionally within the state’s jurisdiction); Municipalities of 
Groton v. FERC, 587 F.2d 1296, 1303 (D.C. Cir. 1978) (finding the Commission’s capacity deficiency charge does 
not encroach on state jurisdiction, even though it may “motivate [utilities] to develop sufficient capacity to meet 
their load requirements”). 
26 Illustrative Tariff, Part XI, § 710.3 (“Transmission Provider will coordinate with the affected Transmission 
Owner(s) to complete studies, including load integration studies, which will provide data relevant to the 
determination of whether (and to what level as applicable) (i) Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service can be 
reliably provided and identify any necessary enhancements to the Transmission System to accommodate the 
requested level of service, and/or (ii) Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Services can be reliably provided.”)  
27 16 U.S.C. § 825l(a) (upon a request for rehearing, “the Commission shall have power to grant or deny rehearing or 
to abrogate or modify its order without further hearing”). 
28 16 U.S.C. § 824d(c) (“[E]very public utility shall file with the Commission … all rates and charges for any 
transmission or sale subject to the jurisdiction of the Commission, and the classifications, practices, and regulations 
affecting such rates and charges, together with all contracts which in any manner affect or relate to such rates, 
charges, classifications, and services.”); Fla. Mun. Power Agency v. Duke Energy Fla., LLC, 167 FERC ¶ 61,138, 
at P 43 (2019) (finding an “unwritten policy constitutes a practice that significantly affects the terms and conditions 
of transmission service … and, therefore, should have been filed with the Commission for Commission review.”). 
29 See supra note 22.

8 
Transmission System.30 Similarly, PJM claims that limiting Non-Firm Contract Demand Service 
to times when the Co-Located Generating Facility is on outage is “appropriate” because of 
unidentified “reliability and operational issues inherent in providing this service.”31 The 
Commission should reject both. 
A. PJM’s Proposed Disqualification and Suspension Scheme is Not a Just, 
Reasonable and Non-Discriminatory Replacement Rate 
PJM fails to demonstrate that “unique reliability and resource adequacy risks” justify the 
extreme and unprecedented penalties PJM proposes with respect to the Commission’s new 
transmission services.  
First, existing practice shows that PJM’s proposal is unwarranted. PJM Transmission 
Customers taking Non-Firm Point-To-Point Transmission Service are not subject to suspension or 
disqualification for unreserved use of the transmission system.32 PJM provides no reason why 
customers taking the new non-firm transmission services should be treated any differently. 
Notably, SPP proposes no suspension or disqualification of interruptible loads as part of its 
Conditional High Impact Large Loads Service (“CHILLS”).33 If SPP can manage interruptible 
loads without such draconian penalties, PJM should similarly be capable of doing so.  
Second, the one reliability incident that PJM highlights to defend its proposal—when 
“approximately 1,500 MW of data centers disconnected simultaneously and unexpectedly from 
the [Bulk Electric System] due to a transmission line fault in 2024”34—involved traditional grid 
30 PJM Apr. 24 Response at 45. 
31 Id. at 6. 
32 Constellation Mar. 25 Reply at 19-20. 
33 Id.
34 PJM Apr. 24 Response at 41-42.

9 
connected load, not a Co-Located Load.35 In fact, this incident illustrates how co-locating load 
with generation can provide benefits to the grid as compared to direct grid connections. As former 
PJM Chief Operating Officer Michael Kormos previously explained, “had those data centers been 
co-located with a generator (especially a nuclear generator), it is possible that the load would not 
have dropped offline as a result of the load being closer to the voltage source.”36
Third, PJM fails to explain how its resource adequacy concerns justify its disqualification 
and suspension scheme. To the extent PJM’s resource adequacy concerns stem from Interim NITS 
and Non-Firm Contract Demand Service being non-capacity backed,37 then PJM should have the 
same concern regarding the non-capacity backed loads that could be interconnected under its 
Connect and Manage framework and would be required to curtail during capacity shortfalls. But 
PJM has proposed no such penalties under the Connect and Manage framework, showing that 
PJM’s real agenda here is to discourage use of the transmission services it disfavors.38
Fourth, a four-month suspension is not “consistent” with NERC requirements as PJM 
claims.39 The NERC Reliability Standards that PJM cites—PRC-004-6 (Protection System 
Misoperation Identification and Correction) and PRC-012-2 (Remedial Action Schemes)—set 
forth a process for investigating whether protection systems misoperated and for developing a 
Corrective Action Plan if appropriate.40 Neither Reliability Standard, however, calls for suspension 
35 Constellation Apr. 23, 2025 Answer, Exhibit 5, at ¶ 7 (Kormos Affidavit). 
36 Id.
37 See infra pp. 13-14 (explaining the Commission rejected the previously proposed Option 7 that provided non-
capacity backed loads would have been interconnected on the condition they would be curtailed before all other load 
during capacity shortfalls).  
38 See generally Connect & Manage Presentation. 
39 PJM Apr. 24 Response at 40. 
40 See, e.g., Reliability Standard PRC-004-6, Protection System Misoperation and Identification, at R1 (“Each 
Transmission Owner, Generator Owner, and Distribution Provider that owns a BES interrupting device that operated

10 
or disqualification of service while an investigation is ongoing. Indeed, such a suspension would 
be fundamentally unjust and unreasonable, as it would deny the load a service to which it is 
entitled—potentially with ruinous economic consequences—without any finding of fault. 
B. Limiting Non-Firm Contract Demand Service to Temporary Derates or 
Outages Is Non-Compliant and Unreasonable 
PJM claims it must limit Non-Firm Contract Demand Service to temporary derates or 
outages because of “the inherent risks to the Transmission System and operational complexities 
associated with providing this service on a continuous basis.”41 Based on this logic, PJM should 
also limit Non-Firm Point-to-Point Transmission Service. PJM does not. Indeed, if the customer 
taking Non-Firm Point-to-Point Transmission Service is willing to pay through congestion, under 
the Transmission Loading Relief Procedure, PJM only curtails the service after all other measures 
have failed to maintain system reliability.42
The Transmission Owners’ attempt to support PJM’s limitation on Non-Firm Contract 
Demand Service fares no better. Citing several of PJM’s unsubstantiated claims, Transmission 
Owners state, “facilities serving large loads will likely have multiple feeders serving load” that 
under the circumstances in Parts 1.1 through 1.3 shall, within 120 calendar days of the BES interrupting device 
operation, identify whether its Protection System component(s) caused a Misoperation ….”); id. at R5 (“Each 
Transmission Owner, Generator Owner, and Distribution Provider that owns the Protection System component(s) 
that caused the Misoperation shall, within 60 calendar days of first identifying a cause of the Misoperation: … 
Develop a Corrective Action Plan (CAP) for the identified Protection System component(s), and an evaluation of 
the CAP’s applicability to the entity’s other Protection Systems including other locations” or “Explain in a 
declaration why corrective actions are beyond the entity’s control or would not improve BES reliability, and that no 
further corrective actions will be taken.”); Reliability Standard PRC-012-2, Remedial Action Schemes, at R5 (“Each 
RAS-entity, within 120 full calendar days of a RAS operation or a failure of its RAS to operate when expected, or 
on a mutually agreed upon schedule with its reviewing Reliability Coordinator(s), shall” “Participate in analyzing 
the RAS operational performance to determine whether” the “System events and/or conditions appropriately 
triggered the RAS,” the “RAS responded as designed,” the “RAS was effective in mitigating BES performance 
issues it was designed to address,” or the “RAS operation resulted in any unintended or adverse BES response.”). 
41 PJM Apr. 24 Response at 7. 
42 PJM Manual 13, § 5.6.

11 
will “add[] complexity and reduc[e] the reliability and overall security of the system.”43 PJM and 
Transmission Owners continue to provide no justification or explanation for requiring multiple 
feeders.44
Transmission Owners also claim “there is the possibility of interactions between RAS in a 
tightly coupled network such as PJM, increasing the possibility of misoperations.”45 This 
circumstance is possible but unlikely. Multiple RAS in an area is a sign the transmission 
infrastructure is inadequate and the area has increased reliability risks. As Mr. Kormos explained, 
“[g]iven the increased reliability risks … most Co-Location Arrangements with new generation 
are unlikely to locate in areas without robust transmission.”46
IV.
The Transmission Owners’ Grid Reliance Charge is Based Neither on Principle Nor 
Precedent 
The Commission should reject the Transmission Owners’ Grid Reliance Charge and adopt 
the minimum system method as recommended by electricity market expert Zachary Ming.47 The 
Transmission Owners’ Grid Reliance Charge is arbitrary and unmoored from cost causation 
principles. As Mr. Ming explains in his Reply Testimony in Attachment 1, the Transmission 
Owners’ proposal is “an improvised approach lacking any theoretical foundation and disconnected 
from any cost-causation principle, designed to produce an outcome that ‘feels right’ to the 
Transmission Owners.”48 Their proposal includes all the depreciation costs for the full cost of 
43 Indicated TO Apr. 24 Response at 4-5. 
44 Constellation Mar. 25 Reply at 30. 
45 Indicated TO Apr. 24 Response at 5. 
46 Constellation Apr. 24 Response, Exhibit 1, at ¶ 11 (“Second Affidavit of Michael Kormos”). 
47 Constellation Mar. 25 Reply, Attachment 1 (“Ming Initial Testimony”). 
48 See Reply Testimony of Zachary Ming at 10:18-20 (“Ming Reply Testimony”).

12 
sizing the transmission system components to serve peak load.49 This would force customers that 
do not impose demand on the grid to pay for transmission components that are sized to serve peak 
load.50 The Transmission Owners’ proposal also arbitrarily excludes costs related to rate of return 
and taxes.51
Constellation’s proposal leverages the minimum system method, a principled methodology 
grounded in precedent, to produce a just and reasonable rate that ensures Co-Located Loads pay 
their fair share of the transmission system based on how they actually use it—which is to receive 
ancillary services, not to draw power from the grid. The minimum system method is a “well-
accepted framework for applying cost-causation principles.”52 It is not “extremely challenging to 
implement.”53 Numerous jurisdictions across North America have applied the minimum system 
method at the distribution level for decades.54 And as Mr. Ming explains, “[t]here is no reason that 
it cannot similarly be applied in the context of the transmission system—there has just not 
previously been any need to do so.”55
In his initial testimony, using publicly available data, Mr. Ming estimated that a minimum 
system yielding between 2% and 10% of actual system costs is reasonable, and he recommended 
a minimum transmission system of 6%.56 The Commission can adopt a Grid Reliance Charge 
based on 6%, or up to 10%, of the NITS rate as a reasonable rate that can be practically

50 Id. at 14:1-5. 
51 Id. at 8:7-12. 
52 Id. at 10:8-15. 
53 Indicated TO Apr. 24 Response at 24. 
54 Ming Reply Testimony at 18:7-11. 
55 Id. at 14:12-14.

implemented. If the Commission believes there should be additional consideration of what 
constitutes a minimum system, the Commission can direct PJM to conduct a minimum system 
study. But the Commission should reject the Transmission Owners’ unsupported and inflated 
proposal. 
V.
Requested Clarifications of PJM’s Response Brief and Modifications to Revised 
Illustrative Tariff 
There are five areas in PJM’s response brief and revised Illustrative Tariff where 
clarification is needed or appropriate. 
First, PJM’s statement that an “Interim NITS customer would only be curtailed … if the 
system is in an unreliable state due to transmission system violations or capacity/reserve 
shortages”57 improperly conflates Interim NITS and the rejected Option 7.58 Under the rejected 
Option 7, non-capacity backed loads would have been interconnected on the condition they would 
be curtailed before all other load during capacity shortfalls.59 The Commission found this option 
“too broad and not sufficiently detailed to direct as a replacement rate.”60 No party, including PJM, 
sought rehearing challenging the Commission’s rejection. PJM now attempts to reinstate the 
“capacity/reserve shortage” curtailment criterion. But PJM failed to seek rehearing of this issue 
and cannot bypass the Federal Power Act’s rehearing requirements.61 The Commission should 
reject this attempt62 and direct PJM to revise Part XI, Section 705.2 of its Illustrative Tariff to 
57 PJM Apr. 24 Response at 20 (emphasis added); see also id. 18 (“Interim NITS must be designed to allow PJM to 
maintain system reliability—both from a transmission and capacity perspective.”). 
58 December 18th Order, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 202. 
59 PJM Answer to February 2025 Show Cause at 18-19 (March 24, 2025). 
60 December 18th Order, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 202. 
61 16 U.S.C. § 825l(a). 
62 See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 195 FERC ¶ 61,030, at P 27 (2026) (rejecting PJM attempt to change a 
Commission-directed definition through its compliance filing because, among other things, “no party, including

14 
specify that Interim NITS shall only be curtailed before Firm Contract Demand Service and NITS 
if the system is in an unreliable state due to transmission system violations. During capacity/reserve 
shortages, like all other loads, Co-Located Loads taking Interim NITS should only be curtailed 
after PJM has taken all real-time emergency procedure steps and still cannot provide adequate 
capacity to meet PJM’s load. 
Second, Constellation supports PJM’s statement that “Eligible Customers serving Co-
Located Loads with pending NITS applications would be able to apply for Interim NITS.”63 PJM 
should revise its Illustrative Tariff accordingly to clarify that large loads with currently pending 
NITS applications shall be studied for Interim NITS at the request of the load without the need to 
make a new or separate application, as long as such loads with pending NITS applications are Co-
Located Loads that will be served by an Eligible Customer. PJM should add such language to 
Section 702.2 (Application Procedures) of Part XI of its Illustrative Tariff. 
Third, PJM should add to the “Conditions Precedent for Receiving Service” in Part XI, 
Subpart A, Section 702.1 and Part XI, Subpart B, Section 710.1 the requirement that the Eligible 
Customer identify the Co-Located Arrangement, including the Customer Facilities that will be 
associated with the Co-Located Load for which the Eligible Customer is taking the service. If the 
Customer Facilities include an existing generator, certification that the existing generator supports 
the request should also be required. This clarification will ensure the Co-Located Load “is 
PJM, sought rehearing or clarification of this directive”); see also, e.g., Ne. Utils. Serv. Co., 74 FERC ¶ 61,355, at 
n.10 (1996).

physically connected to the facilities of an existing or planned Customer Facility,” consistent with 
the definition of Co-Located Load.64
